1000171.etyen:
From bo (“to live, dwell”), from Old Norse búa (“to live, dwell”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *būaną (“to dwell, live, cultivate”). In botanical terminology, the element is used with prefixes such as en- (“one”), sam- (“together, same”), sær- (“separate”) and tve- (“two”) to describe whether male and female reproductive organs occur on the same plant or on separate plants.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk -bu and Danish -bo (“botany suffix”).

1001451.etyen:
Internationalism, ultimately from Latin Ganymēdēs (“Ganymede”), from Ancient Greek Γανυμήδης (Ganumḗdēs, “Ganymede”). The Ancient Greek name was already interpreted in antiquity as being connected with γάνυμαι (gánumai, “to rejoice, be glad”) and μήδεα (mḗdea, “plans, thoughts, counsel”), an interpretation implied by Socrates in Xenophon's Symposium (8.29–30); the actual formation of the name is not certain.
The astronomical name is an eponym of the mythological figure. The moon was discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610. Simon Marius proposed the name Ganymedes in 1614, one of four names sugge
